Lee Yeow Seng: The Malaysian tycoon playing the long game in Singapore
article:
Lee Yeow Seng likens IOI Properties Group ’s moves in Singapore to “playing a chess game”. Over the years, he has placed the group’s pieces across the city centre: IOI Central Boulevard Towers, South Beach , Asia Square Tower 2 , Shenton House and the upcoming  W Residences Marina View — Singapore. His next move is One Raffles Place .

For spearheading IOI Properties Group’s aggressive expansion in Singapore, Lee was named Personality of the Year at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026. And he is still buying. “We have a strong footprint here, and it makes sense for us to build on it,” he says.

Singapore is familiar ground for the 47-year-old. Lee came to Singapore at 13 to attend St Patrick’s School first, then Tampines Meridian Junior College. Following in the footsteps of his elder brother, Lee Yeow Chor, group managing director and chief executive of IOI Group, he read law at King’s College London, earning an LLB (Honours) before being called to the Bar of England and Wales. He then spent two years at ING Private Bank in Singapore.

Get the latest details on available units and prices for W Residences Marina View - Singapore

“I spent eight years of my childhood and adulthood here, so I know Singapore very well,” says Lee, group CEO of Malaysia-listed IOI Properties Group since January 2014. He and his brother ranked third on Forbes ’ 2026 list of Malaysia’s 50 richest, with a combined net worth of US$8.5 billion ($10.9 billion).

In early October, IOI and CapitaLand Investment were reported to be in exclusive talks to jointly acquire One Raffles Place on a 50:50 basis for about $2.3 billion to $2.4 billion. Seller OUE Reit has confirmed the exclusivity, with due diligence underway, but says no binding agreement has been signed as yet.

A prime address

One Raffles Place comprises the 62-storey Tower 1, formerly OUB Centre, completed in 1986 on an 841-year leasehold plot; and the 38-storey Tower 2, with a six-storey retail podium completed in 2012. The complex has a net lettable area (NLA) of about 875,000 sq ft and sits atop Raffles Place MRT Interchange Station (for the North-South and East-West lines).

“I’m attracted by the address,” says Lee. “I worked at Republic Plaza for two years when I was with ING, so I know the location very well.”

Raffles Place has long been Singapore’s financial district. Local banks UOB and OCBC are headquartered there, while foreign banks including Malaysia’s CIMB, France’s BNP Paribas and US bank JPMorgan have their Singapore offices in the area.

Lee also sees an opportunity to enhance the area’s F&B offerings. “Raffles Place lacks retail space and eateries,” he says. “At lunchtime on weekdays, it’s still very crowded. I think we can offer much more interesting and better dining options.”

Longer term, he sees potential to redevelop Tower 1 or carry out a major asset enhancement initiative (AEI). Asking rents for office space at One Raffles Place currently range from $11 to $13.50 psf per month, according to Corporate Locations. Lee believes an AEI or redevelopment could bring them up to par with IOI Central Boulevard Towers in Marina Bay.

Setting the office benchmark

IOI won the Central Boulevard site in a Government Land Sale tender in November 2016 with a top bid of $2.57 billion. Completed in 1Q2024, IOI Central Boulevard Towers has 1.26 million sq ft of office space across two towers. It was valued at $4.4 billion at the start of 2026, up from a projected gross development value (GDV) of $3.5 billion in 2017.

The development is now 98% committed, with asking rents at $18 psf per month. “When we started, rents were only in the early teens,” says Lee. “As we ramped up occupancy, we saw rents go up to close to $20 psf.”

He attributes the rise to a flight to quality. “People want to move to the newest and greenest building. It’s an ESG thing for a lot of multinational companies. It’s also easier for them to recruit and retain talent.”

Raffles Place’s older towers are being renewed to keep up. Singapore Land Group (SingLand) completed a $160 million AEI at Singapore Land Tower in 2025, while City Developments Ltd ’s (CDL) Republic Plaza underwent a $70 million AEI in 2018 and 2019. SingLand is also redeveloping the former Clifford Centre site into The Clifford, a 35-storey office tower due for completion in 2028.

With the rejuvenation of Raffles Place underway, Lee believes “it’s the right time for us to acquire a prominent building there”.

Building a downtown network

In April, IOI acquired the office component of Asia Square Tower 2 at Marina Bay from CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust for $2.476 billion. The building is linked at the second level to IOI Central Boulevard Towers.

Then there is Shenton House, which Lee bought in his personal capacity through Shenton 101 for $538 million in a collective sale tender in November 2023. On Oct 1, IOI agreed to acquire Shenton 101 for a nominal $1, taking on its borrowings and settling about $217 million in shareholder advances from Lee. The site will be redeveloped into premium offices and a luxury hotel. Once completed, it will link to Asia Square Tower 2 on the other side.

Together, the three buildings will form a connected downtown network. “If we combine IOI Central Boulevard Towers, Asia Square Tower 2 and Shenton House, we actually have three very prominent office buildings in the CBD,” says Lee. “So we can offer our tenants different services and different floor plates to cater to their needs.”

Holding firm at W Residences

IOI’s other Marina Bay project is taking shape on the Marina View white site, which it acquired in September 2021 for $1.508 billion. Scheduled for completion in 1Q2029, the 51-storey development will comprise the 683-unit W Residences Marina View and the 360-room W Singapore — Marina View hotel, with sheltered and underground connections to three MRT stations.

For Lee, the appeal lies in downtown living. “When it’s completed, you can live, work and play here,” he says. “You can party at the W hotel, and if you’re bored, you can walk to Marina Bay Sands . Downtown is actually a very nice place to live, even for families.”

Since its launch in October 2025, W Residences Marina View has sold 15 units (2.2%) as at Nov 3, at prices ranging from $1.88 million to $10.9 million. On a psf basis, prices ranged from $2,609 to $4,256 psf, with an average price of $3,082 psf.

Despite the slow sales, Lee says the group has no intention of cutting prices. “We are going to just bite the bullet and complete the units,” he says. “Eventually, we will rent them out, and they will form part of our investment properties, as we did at Sentosa Cove .”

Holding on to the units comes at a cost. Under Singapore’s additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) rules, developers can obtain an upfront remission of part of the tax on residential land, provided they complete the project and sell all units within five years.

For the Marina View site, bought in September 2021, that remission is 25% of the land price. If the deadline is missed, the remitted amount must be repaid, with interest.

Lee told Bloomberg he has secured a temporary reprieve from the Singapore authorities until April 2027 and will continue appealing against the charge.

‘Market anomaly’

Lee points to what he calls “an anomaly” in the market: suburban projects are now priced close to city-centre developments. In Jurong West, the 99-year leasehold private condo, Lucerne Grand , sold 350 (61.4%) of its 570 units at its launch weekend in early October. Analysts expect the upcoming 99-year leasehold condo at New Upper Changi Road to average $2,900 to $3,000 psf, close to what W Residences Marina View has achieved.

The reason, he says, is the 60% ABSD imposed on foreign buyers, which has suppressed demand for homes in the CBD. “But I think it’s just a matter of time before people realise that the value of living in the city centre should be higher than that of living in a suburban location,” he adds.

Lee believes Singapore buyers have yet to fully appreciate the convenience of living in a hotel-branded residence.

W Residences Marina View is the first branded residence in Singapore integrated with a hotel in the same tower.

Earlier hotel-branded residences have separate residential and hotel buildings. St Regis Residences is connected underground to its namesake hotel, while The Residences at W Singapore Sentosa Cove sits beside the W Singapore — Sentosa Cove hotel.

“We can provide concierge, butler service, room service and housekeeping,” says Lee. “We can even walk your dog if you’re too busy, or take care of your apartment if you’re not around.”

Lee also sees a distinction in the lifestyle offered. “The Residences at W Singapore Sentosa Cove is very much a resort, while W Residences Marina View will be very much about city living,” he says. “Residents will be able to watch the F1 race from home. Marina Bay Sands Tower 4, with its new MICE facilities and concert arena, will be just a 10-minute walk away.”

Marina View is part of a wider bet on the W brand. IOI also owns W Kuala Lumpur and recently signed an agreement with Marriott International to develop W Langkawi, slated to open by 2029. “I like the W brand because it’s very much a lifestyle brand — very trendy, very high-end and very hip,” says Lee. “I’m relatively young as well, so I like the kind of vibe the W has.”

Where it began: Sentosa Cove

IOI made its first major property investments in Singapore at Sentosa Cove, a luxury waterfront residential enclave targeted at international buyers. Lee recalls how his father, the late Lee Shin Cheng, founder of IOI, was “very good friends” with fellow tycoon Chua Thian Poh, founder of Ho Bee Land . In 2007, the two friends formed a 50:50 joint venture to bid for a site that became the 151-unit Seascape.

In January 2008, Ho Bee and IOI won the last condo site at Sentosa Cove, this time with IOI holding a 65% stake. It became the 302-unit Cape Royale, the enclave’s largest condo, with blocks of up to 20 storeys. When it was completed in 2013, the partners leased out the units rather than sell them in a falling market, only launching them for sale in 2022.

Across both developments, about half the units have been sold, with the remainder leased out, notes Lee.

“The rental market at Sentosa Cove is quite active,” he says. In August, a sky villa at Cape Royale, measuring between 8,400 and 8,500 sq ft, was leased for $40,000 a month, according to URA Realis data.

The top-floor units offer uninterrupted sea views. “When you’re up there, you don’t even feel like you’re in Singapore. It feels like a tropical resort somewhere else,” says Lee. “You feel like you’re in your own world.”

The South Beach deal

Lee says he was involved in all of IOI’s property deals in Singapore, but South Beach was the one he handled personally, which is why he still remembers the details so well.

A consortium of CDL, Dubai World’s investment arm Istithmar, and Israeli developer Elad Group won the site in 2007, each holding a one-third stake.

When the global financial crisis struck in 2008, Istithmar and Elad were forced to seek buyers for their stakes.

In 2011, JLL, acting for Istithmar, approached IOI. The group took a 49.9% stake and became CDL’s partner in jointly developing South Beach.

In June 2025, IOI agreed to buy out CDL’s 50.1% stake for $834.2 million, based on an agreed property value of $2.75 billion. “It has been quite a journey,” says Lee.

He points to South Beach, completed in 2016, as proof that IOI can deliver “a very high-quality project in Singapore”. “Today, the property is still very well-maintained by us,” he says.

South Beach Residences, W Residences Marina View and IOI’s Sentosa Cove condos are all on 99-year leases. Lease decay may worry some buyers, but not Lee.

“Ninety-nine years is not a short time — it will probably last two generations, so you can still pass it on to your children,” he says. “Value can still hold up, depending on location and whether you have the right product offering.”

More deals ahead

IOI now holds about $10 billion in wholly owned investment assets in Singapore, and more with Shenton House, but Lee is already lining up his next moves. On Oct 15, he told Bloomberg that IOI was in exclusive talks to acquire Chijmes and the nearby Capitol Kempinski Hotel Singapore on Stamford Road, though he declined to disclose the price. Chijmes was valued at $379 million at the end of 2025, while the hotel had reportedly been marketed for about $600 million.

A day later, IOI clarified in a bourse filing that its board had yet to deliberate on the potential acquisitions.

The rapid expansion has come at a cost: IOI’s net debt stood at about 85% of equity at end-June, according to Bloomberg. Lee aims to bring that down to between 30% and 50% within three to five years.

To unlock capital, IOI has started marketing a private fund comprising IOI Central Boulevard Towers and the office component of South Beach, valued at about $6 billion, which it expects to launch in the next few months. Selling a 50% stake in the fund could raise nearly $3.14 billion, Lee said on Nov 3.

The longer-term aim is to list the fund as a Reit. Lee is also eyeing a secondary listing of IOI on the Singapore Exchange in early 2027, though the group said in October that the plan had yet to be put to its board.

For Lee, the logic behind his Singapore strategy remains simple. “For the property business, it’s all about location, location, location,” he says. “If you want to make your mark, you definitely want to go for the most prominent and most prime locations.”

Retail’s new centre of gravity

Orchard Road has lost some of its appeal for Lee. “I feel like the centre of gravity has moved away from Orchard Road,” he says. “I don’t feel as attracted to Orchard Road as I was when I was a student 30 years ago.” Instead, he sees Marina Bay Sands, with its luxury mall The Shoppes, as the new magnet for high-end shoppers.

He also considers Singapore’s retail rents “too high”. “After paying these high rents, retailers have little margin left,” he says.

Lee’s views are shaped by his experience in retail. He joined IOI Properties in 2011 as head of marketing and leasing for IOI City Mall in Putrajaya. With 2.5 million sq ft of NLA, the mall is more than twice the size of VivoCity, Singapore’s largest shopping mall, and IOI plans to add another million sq ft.

Apple is set to open its second store in Malaysia at IOI City Mall, says Lee. It first opened at The Exchange TRX in Kuala Lumpur in June 2024. “When Apple chooses your location, it shows that you must have done something right, because they are very, very selective,” he says.

For Lee, attracting retailers comes down to understanding shoppers. “Retail is all about the shoppers and footfall,” he says. “Our footfall at IOI City Mall has been increasing by double digits every year since we opened the mall in 2014.”

Eyes on Johor

Lee is also closely watching the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone. IOI has been in Johor for three decades. Its active land bank there carries an estimated GDV of RM6.8 billion ($2.15 billion), according to its 3QFY2026 results presentation, with a further 1,481 acres (599ha) in Segamat and Tangkak held for future development.

He says Johor is attracting renewed interest from Singapore investors, mainland Chinese capital and American companies exploring data-centre and AI opportunities. “We have always been there,” he says. “So when the interest comes, we stand to benefit from it.”

Singapore, however, remains his main focus. “You want to invest in a country that is stable and transparent, with good governance and stable policies,” says Lee. “Singapore fits all these criteria.”

“I’m more optimistic about Singapore than Singaporeans are,” he adds.

title: JTC powers Singapore's sustainable industrial future, from untapped solar potential to adaptive reuse
article:
The void spaces between Singapore’s industrial buildings could potentially be used to generate solar energy, while Jurong Island is being developed as a testbed for new low-carbon technologies.

Adaptive reuse also continues to gain ground as more existing industrial buildings are repurposed to meet new needs.

These are among the ways that JTC is working to make the country's industrial estates more sustainable and ready for future industries.

Its efforts have earned the government agency the Top Sustainable Developer title for the second year running at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

Bulim Square, an advanced manufacturing development by JTC in the Jurong Innovation District, was also named Top Industrial Development (Non-Central) at this year’s awards.

"As JTC plans and builds the industrial spaces that will power Singapore’s economy, sustainability is an important part of preparing for that future," says Jacqueline Poh, CEO of the statutory board, at the awards ceremony.

As Singapore's industrial master planner and developer, JTC anticipates how industries will develop, the infrastructure they will need, as well as how best to use the country's limited land, energy and resources.

This means making existing developments more sustainable, while pioneering and scaling new ways to design, build and rejuvenate industrial spaces for the future.

"For JTC, sustainability is fundamentally about preparing for what’s next," says David Tan, its assistant CEO.

Harnessing more solar energy across industrial estates

JTC has facilitated solar installations at more than 800 privately leased industrial properties.

That has delivered a total solar capacity of about 875 megawatt-peak (MWp) across its estates.

These are expected to generate enough renewable electricity to power more than 204,000 four-room HDB flats annually, while reducing carbon emissions by over 375,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent each year.

Such large-scale deployment is possible through JTC's efforts to pool demand, provide common infrastructure and bring together companies, technology providers and public agencies.

"Many sustainability opportunities become more viable when pursued collectively," says Tan.

"This enables solutions to be implemented as a scale that individual companies may not be able to achieve on their own."

To build on these efforts, JTC is also working to unlock more space for solar generation — including making all feasible rooftops and temporary land plots available for solar photovoltaic (PV) installations.

It is also exploring less conventional spaces, such as the void spaces between multi-storey industrial buildings. In December 2025, JTC launched a pilot at 15 Woodlands Loop to test this concept with Singapore’s first overhang solar PV system.

The project’s first stage involves the design, construction, operation and testing over a 15-month period.

It targets a capacity of at least 250 kWp across about 4,300 sq m (46,285 sq ft) of previously untapped space. The findings will then help JTC assess whether similar overhang PV systems can be installed and scaled at other industrial estates.

Jurong Island's next chapter in low-carbon technologies

Jurong Island, a cornerstone of Singapore's energy and chemicals sector, is transforming into a hub for sustainable materials and a global testbed for new energies and low-carbon technologies.

Low-carbon solutions — ranging from carbon capture, utilisation and storage; electrification and energy efficiency; to circular plastics — are being piloted and scaled across the island.

Close to 300ha of land on Jurong Island has been set aside for next-generation energy infrastructure, including hydrogen, ammonia, sustainable aviation fuel and advanced battery systems.

Another 20ha has been set aside for Singapore’s largest low-carbon data centre park, with a capacity of up to 700 megawatts (MW), Tan highlights.

Powering this refreshed direction are multiple partnerships that began in November 2025.

"These studies and collaborations span areas such as low-carbon energy infrastructure, more energy- and water-efficient data centres, and access to global climate-tech solutions," he adds.

One of the tie-ups is between JTC and Keppel to jointly study shared cooling, thermal storage and the use of waste heat, to pilot district-level energy and thermal infrastructure across Jurong Island.

JTC is also working with the National University of Singapore to study a new data-centre testbed facility on the island, where data-centre operators can trial AI-ready, low-carbon technologies such as liquid cooling and predictive energy management.

Another initiative is the new $62.5 million Low-Carbon Technology Translational Testbed (LCT3), which broke ground on Oct 23 this year, by the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*Star).

Located on Jurong Island, the A*Star facility will help companies test and scale emerging low-carbon technologies for industrial use towards commercial deployment.

Making sustainability integral to operations

Different industries have varying requirements for energy, logistics, buildings and infrastructure.

JTC takes these needs into account when planning its industrial districts. It combines passive building design, technology and shared infrastructure to reduce resource use while supporting business growth and innovation.

"Rather than treating sustainability as a standalone feature, we design it into the way districts operate," Tan says.

He cites Bulim Square and Punggol Digital District (PDD) as examples of how district-level planning can bring both sustainability and operational benefits.

By tapping shared infrastructure and energy-efficient systems, companies in these districts can operate more sustainably.

Buildings are also designed to maximise natural light, reduce solar heat gain and improve airflow. Other sustainability features include district cooling, solar generation, rainwater harvesting and lush landscaping.

At Bulim Square, companies have access to about 110,000 sq m of BCA Green Mark Platinum-certified advanced manufacturing space.

Bulim Square also connects to Jurong Innovation District’s underground District Logistics Network (DLN), which is designed to improve logistics efficiency while reducing vehicular traffic at street level.

Meanwhile, PDD, which will officially open in December 2026, features Singapore’s first district-level smart grid integrating a battery energy storage system with solar photovoltaic panels.

Using real-time data management and renewable energy generation, the system is meant to optimise energy efficiency across PDD.

Taking innovation to scale

"The value of a new solution lies in its ability to move beyond a successful trial into wider use," says Tan.

JTC's industrial estates 'provide real operating environments" where companies can validate their technologies under actual working conditions, he adds.

Its pipeline of developments also offers opportunities for proven solutions to be adopted across more projects.

One example is the Decarbonisation Living Lab programme, which supports the co-innovation of new solutions to energy consumption in buildings.

Under the programme, two projects are being trialled at CleanTech One, which is part of CleanTech Park in the Jurong Innovation District. The development houses offices, workshops and laboratories for cleantech-related R&D activities.

Meanwhile, JTC is also testing solutions to detect early water leakage, through AI-driven anomaly analytics, Tan shares.

To help promising technologies progress beyond the testing stage, the agency introduced several measures this year to help construction technologies progress from testing to deployment.

These include the Innovative Procurement Partnership, which allows technologies that have been successfully piloted to be deployed in other JTC projects without going through a fresh tender process.

Another new initiative is the Integrated Digital Delivery Technology Alliance, which gives project partners access to vetted digital solutions.

Old buildings, new possibilities

Repurposing old industrial buildings can offer a more sustainable way to make space for new uses, reducing the need for new construction.

"Existing structures contain embodied carbon, infrastructure and, in some cases, industrial heritage. Adaptive reuse retains this value while preparing sites for new economic needs," Tan notes.

One of JTC's latest adaptive reuse projects is the upcoming startup hub Kampong AI at LaunchPad @ one-north, where two existing flatted factories will be converted into an integrated work-and-living community for companies and professionals in the AI sector.

One block will house about 14,500 sq m of business park space, including event and collaboration areas, for up to 70 companies. The adjacent block will provide more than 200 residential units, allowing the startup community to both live and work in Kampong AI.

Targeted for completion in 2028, Kampong AI will give the existing buildings a new purpose while supporting the growth of Singapore's AI ecosystem.

Another example of adaptive reuse is the Industrial Government Land Sales (IGLS) site along Kallang Way, which has since progressed from tender to redevelopment.

Set to become Gourmet Xchange, an integrated waterfront food hub by CapitaLand Development , the site included an 1980s, first-generation terraced factory cluster, which is now being adapted for food production, research and related activities as the development’s low-rise Heritage Terrace block.

The retention and repurposing of the existing building was a requirement of the IGLS tender, given the site’s historical and cultural significance, as well as to reduce carbon emissions. CapitaLand Development will preserve the block’s architectural elements including the iconic gable-end wall profiles and protruding solar fins.

"Adaptive reuse starts with understanding what an existing building can contribute to its next use," Tan says.

To maximise the value of what has already been built, JTC’s framework assesses industrial buildings against future industrial needs as well as the social, economic and environmental outcomes they can deliver.

"This complements our broader efforts to retrofit, rejuvenate and redevelop mature industrial spaces so that they remain productive and relevant,” Tan continues.

He adds that in 2025, JTC rejuvenated more than 500,000 sq m of industrial space to “create a comfortable and welcoming environment where industrial communities can thrive".

Building for the next generation of industries

Over the next decade, JTC plans to develop more than 400,000 sq m of new industrial space.

Upcoming projects include AeroSpace4 at Seletar Aerospace Park, as well as new general manufacturing spaces in Ang Mo Kio, Defu, Tuas and Woodlands.

Lessons in planning, design, shared infrastructure, adaptive reuse, renewable energy, smart systems and construction technology continue to inform how these developments are planned and delivered.

Amid pressures from rising energy demand, higher carbon costs and the need to remain competitive, it is becoming increasingly important to productively use energy, land and resources, as well as to scale viable sustainability solutions.

Against this backdrop, Singapore can be where new models for sustainable industry are developed, tested and proven under actual operating conditions, Tan says.

"We build and learn here to strengthen Singapore's industrial competitiveness, while contributing solutions and models that can advance industries around the world."

title: UOL Group sets its sights on large-scale developments and distinctive homes with enduring value
article:
UOL Group has taken home another Top Developer accolade at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026, adding to a year marked by robust residential sales, multiple project awards and the continued expansion of its pipeline.

Three projects in the Singapore-listed property group’s residential portfolio were recognised at this year's EPEA: AMO Residence , UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard , and Skye at Holland .

The slew of wins comes amid exceptional sales performance across its portfolio. Skye at Holland, which moved 99% of its 666 units on the first day of launch in October 2025, has since been fully sold. Watten House and Pinetree Hill also achieved sell-out status in 2026.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

For group CEO Liam Wee Sin, the latest Top Developer award reflects the dedication of UOL's employees and partners, as well as the trust that homebuyers and stakeholders have placed in its UOL Homes brand.

"Property development is a long-term business. The recognition we receive today is the result of years of collective effort and a series of decisions made along the way, from identifying the right sites and opportunities to developing the right products and seeing them through to completion," he says.

UOL describes its development philosophy as grounded in disciplined site selection, thoughtful design and quality execution — honed over many years.

"For us, success is not defined by any single development, but by our ability to consistently deliver quality homes that stand the test of time and continue to be valued by our homebuyers," Liam adds.

Finding the right site and product

Identifying sites with strong fundamentals and creating the right products to maximise their potential are central to UOL’s approach.

Shirley Ng, chief investment and asset officer, notes that the developer considers a site’s intrinsic attributes — such as connectivity, proximity to schools, surrounding amenities, as well as green and blue spaces — and the scarcity of comparable sites.

The group seeks to strike a balance between creativity and prudence in its decisions at every stage, from land acquisition and design through to marketing and project delivery.

"We play an important curatorial role, bringing together the expertise of our development and marketing teams, architects and consultants to ensure that every element contributes to a cohesive and compelling product," Ng says.

"A good development is usually the result of many decisions being iterated and refined until they all work together."

She cites the Dorset Gardens residential project, slated for launch in the first half of 2027, as an example of this approach.

Located in District 8 in the Rest of Central Region or city fringe, the 425-unit condo will be a four-minute walk from Farrer Park MRT Station.

It is set to offer residents convenient access to Orchard Road, the CBD and the Novena healthcare cluster, alongside established retail and lifestyle amenities such as City Square Mall and Piccadilly Galleria.

Families may also be drawn to its proximity to popular schools including Hong Wen School and St Joseph's Institution Junior, both within 1km of Dorset Gardens.

Distinctive homes for different lifestyles

UOL's expertise across residential, commercial and hospitality developments informs how it creates homes where aesthetics, functionality and liveability come together.

The 301-unit UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard drew inspiration from the group’s hospitality portfolio, including the Pan Pacific Orchard hotel, to introduce wellness and hospitality elements into the luxury living experience.

"We also worked closely with our consultants to incorporate a unique combination of double-volume living spaces, private lifts and dedicated parking within the Bespoke Collection," says Anson Lim, senior general manager (residential marketing) of UOL.

These were made possible through innovative applications of prefabricated prefinished volumetric construction, he adds.

At the 226-unit Meyer Blue, another luxury condo, the developers – UOL, together with Singapore Land Group Ltd (SingLand) – sought to make the most of the site’s location in the prime Meyer Road enclave in the east, as well as its unblocked views of the sea and the Marina Bay area.

Bringing across the concept of "Experiential Luxury by the Coast", the project's rooftop Meyer Club, sky gym and outdoor terrace were designed to capitalise on the coastal and city vistas.

These projects also demonstrate how UOL tailors each development to its location and target audience.

"Every location has its own character, and different buyer segments have different lifestyles, aspirations and needs," Lim notes. "Our role is to translate these insights into the right product positioning, unit mix, layouts, amenities and finishes."

He adds that the developer pays attention to not just how its customers live today, but also how their needs and aspirations may evolve over time.

UOL also sees opportunities to tap its diversified portfolio to play a role in the transformation of wider precincts.

For instance, together with Pan Pacific Orchard and the upcoming NoMad Hilton Singapore hotel, UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard is expected to contribute to the ongoing rejuvenation of the Orchard Road shopping belt into a more vibrant destination for residents and visitors.

"Great developments are more than the sum of their parts," Lim says, adding that when it comes to placemaking, the collective impact of several developments can be far greater than their individual contributions.

Understanding what homebuyers value

The group’s recent standout sales performance has also provided further insights into changing homebuyer expectations.

Angeline Fu, deputy general manager (residential marketing) of UOL, observes that buyers are increasingly assessing residential projects more holistically.

They are looking beyond location to also consider factors including layout efficiency, quality of finishes, facilities, pricing and the developer's track record.

"Buyers today are well-informed and discerning," she says. “They are looking for a home that offers the right combination of quality, lifestyle and value.”

The strong response to Skye at Holland, alongside the sell-out of Watten House and Pinetree Hill, has reinforced the importance of matching the right product to the intended market.

"Staying close to the ground is essential to understanding shifts in buyer preferences and market sentiment," Fu shares. "These insights allow us to continually refine our offerings, ensuring that our developments remain relevant to evolving customer expectations and are well-positioned to meet market demand."

At the same time, maintaining consistent quality, thoughtfulness and attention to detail, while giving each development its own identity, has helped build trust and loyalty among buyers.

“We believe this is reflected in the strong support from repeat buyers and the continued appeal and resale value of our developments,” Lim says.

Mega projects are resonating with homebuyers

Looking ahead, UOL is placing greater emphasis on large-scale residential developments, which appear to be gaining traction with homebuyers.

"We are seeing growing interest in large-scale developments which offer opportunities for expansive landscaping, extensive facilities, and a wider variety of homes catering to different profiles and lifestyles," Ng says.

This approach can be seen in the group's residential sites and pipeline, including the 1,193-unit Parktown Residence , which moved 1,041 units (87%) at its February 2025 debut; the 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve, which achieved a 90.1% take-up at launch at end-October 2026; an upcoming development of more than 800 homes at Hougang Central; as well as another project with over 1,000 homes at New Upper Changi Road .

Each of these mega projects will offer a distinct proposition for different buyer segments.

"For UOL, leveraging scale is a deliberate strategy to differentiate our product offering, create better residential experience and broaden our market reach," Ng says.

By combining well-located sites with generous spaces and comprehensive facilities, the group aims to create residential experiences that are difficult to replicate.

Confidence in Singapore's prospects

UOL's continued investment in Singapore signals its confidence in the city-state’s long-term fundamentals.

Yvonne Tan, chief corporate and development officer of UOL, points to Singapore’s political and economic stability, safe-haven appeal, population growth, infrastructure investment and strong household balance sheets as factors supporting the property market.

"These structural strengths give us the conviction to continue investing in Singapore while remaining disciplined in our capital allocation," she adds.

Following a strong 2025, the residential property market in Singapore has entered a more balanced phase, characterised by moderate price growth and stable demand-supply dynamics.

Prices of non-landed private homes gained 1% in the third quarter of this year, reversing from the 0.1% decrease in the previous quarter.

UOL anticipates the Singapore residential market staying broadly stable and resilient through the rest of 2026 and into 2027.

"Underlying demand remains healthy, but it is becoming increasingly project-specific, with well-located, well-designed and realistically priced developments continuing to see healthy take-up," Tan says.

Against this backdrop, she highlights the importance of disciplined execution and pipeline replenishment in sustaining long-term growth.

"A successful developer must be able to sell well and replenish well. It is not just about achieving strong sales, but also about consistently identifying the right opportunities for future growth," Tan notes.

Creating value, shaping a sustainable future

As UOL expands its residential pipeline, it is also looking at how its developments can contribute to Singapore's urban transformation.

These efforts are aligned with the group’s vision of creating value and shaping a sustainable future.

"Singapore is a city in transformation, and the built environment plays an important role in shaping how people live, work and connect," Liam says.

"Through our residential developments, we have helped rejuvenate neighbourhoods, while our commercial and hospitality assets have contributed to creating vibrant lifestyle and community spaces across the city."

Sustainability continues to be a key consideration. Across its portfolio, UOL incorporates environmentally responsible design principles and invests in initiatives that support climate resilience and social well-being.

It intends to continue applying its diversified capabilities across different property sectors to shape places that will be “delightfully liveable for generations".

"Ultimately, our aspiration goes beyond building homes or selling units. It is about creating endearing homes and enduring environments that bring people together, enrich their neighbourhoods and continue to be valued for generations," Liam says.

title: From Martin Modern to River Modern: How GuocoLand puts people at the heart of design
article:
A long, narrow land parcel along the Singapore River might look like a constraint for a residential development. GuocoLand Ltd saw it as an opportunity.

The site’s linear shape allowed the developer to space the residential blocks farther apart and maximise river views, says group CEO Cheng Hsing Yao. The result is River Modern , a 455-unit, 99-year leasehold development where about 70% of the apartments face the river.

Demand was swift. About 90% of the units sold over the launch weekend in March, and as at Nov 3, the project was 95.4% sold at an average of $3,290 psf.

The approach reflects the philosophy behind GuocoLand’s residential and mixed-use developments over the past decade. Rather than applying a standard formula, the group identifies each site’s strengths and builds on them.

“In real estate, you cannot be very formulaic,” says Cheng. “It’s methodology more than formula that drives us.”

It is an approach that runs across GuocoLand’s portfolio, from the luxury Martin Modern in prime District 9 and the integrated Guoco Midtown at Beach Road to the Lentor Hills private residential precinct and the nature-inspired Springleaf Residence in the Outside Central Region.

It has earned the group a Top Developer award at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026, its sixth win in the category.

Cheng credits the company’s evolution to a stronger focus on product development, backed by in-house capabilities in land acquisition, design, construction, sales, leasing and property management.

A trained architect, he spent the first 15 years of his career at URA and the Centre for Liveable Cities. He became group managing director of GuocoLand Singapore in 2014 and group CEO in July 2021.

Designing from the inside out

GuocoLand also keeps a close eye on emerging trends, changing lifestyles, and how each property will age over time.

“We have a philosophy that guides all our developments: a strong belief in a product designed for people,” he says. “We call it the inside-out approach. We will not compromise the internal layout to achieve a certain external look.”

In practice, that means paying close attention to the proportions of living and dining rooms, bedrooms, bathrooms, kitchen and utility areas. “The homebuyer is paying for every single square foot of the unit, so we want to make sure that every square foot is as usable as possible,” he says.

Changing lifestyles also shape the design and layouts of its homes. The rise of working from home after the Covid-19 pandemic led GuocoLand to introduce flexible spaces that can serve as a home office, utility room or extra bedroom.

Even robotic vacuum cleaners feature in the design process. In several projects, GuocoLand has built in a nook with a charging point, positioned so the robot cleaner can easily find its way back. That keeps the appliance from ending up in a conspicuous or inconvenient corner, says Cheng.

The same thinking extends to the common areas. Instead of squeezing in as many facilities as possible, GuocoLand prefers amenities large enough to be practical and enjoyable. Landscaping is planned with long-term maintenance and resilience in mind. The developer favours a diverse mix of plant species, including native varieties — like those found in public spaces — over exotic species that may be difficult to maintain over time.

Playing to each site’s strength

Martin Modern marked an important milestone in GuocoLand’s residential design. The group won the 99-year leasehold site at Martin Place in mid-2016, and it was the first project the current management team worked on together.

Designed by Yip Yuen Hong of ip:li Architects with ADDP Architects, its two 30-storey towers have a façade of corrugated pre-cast concrete panels with a burnished brass look. The design pays homage to Robertson Quay’s history as a warehouse district. At the crown of each of the twin 30-storey towers is a “secret garden” with reading areas and dining pavilions.

Martin Modern was also the first in GuocoLand’s “Modern” series, which now includes Midtown Modern , Lentor Modern and River Modern. It introduced the series’ hallmarks: a grand arrival, lush landscaping with a lawn, a view for every unit, and interiors designed for owner-occupiers.

The developments share these hallmarks, but Cheng emphasises that each responds differently to its location and intended residents.

The same site-specific thinking extends beyond the series. Springleaf Residence sits on land that was once part of the Nee Soon Swamp Forest, next to the Central Catchment Nature Reserve. The site also includes a block of the former Upper Thomson Secondary School, built in 1965, which had to be conserved.

For GuocoLand, the forest and the old school were the very reasons to bid for the site, along with its location right in front of Springleaf MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line. The developer designed the project around them. A nature corridor along the boundary allows birds and wildlife to move between the forest and the reserve, while the towers are oriented to take in views of greenery and the reservoirs.

The conserved block has been converted into 32 apartments, and the school’s heritage inspired the development’s theme. In front of it, a lawn resembling a school field is ringed by a jogging track. Opposite is the ECA House, named after the extra-curricular activities of the past, now known as co-curricular activities. The nostalgic touch resonated with Gen X buyers, who made up a large share of purchasers.

“We built a certain sense of heritage and community around the concept of school,” says Cheng.

Moving into new precincts

Cheng believes the definition of a prime residential location has become more nuanced as Singapore’s MRT network expands and new precincts emerge. Convenience, he argues, should not be measured purely by distance.

A suburban home with direct MRT access may be more convenient than one closer to the city that requires switching between different modes of public transport.

It is why GuocoLand bought into Lentor Hills and Springleaf, where its developments sit right next to MRT stations.

At Lentor Hills estate, GuocoLand was a first mover. It won the first site released for sale in April 2021, which became Lentor Modern. The project has 605 units across three blocks above a retail mall that includes a 10,000 sq ft supermarket and a 12,000 sq ft childcare centre, linked directly to Lentor MRT Station (Thomson-East Coast Line).

In March, a consortium of GuocoLand, Hong Leong Holdings and TID won the eighth site URA has launched at the estate, with a bid of $657.1 million, or $1,267 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr). It is GuocoLand’s fifth Lentor Hills site and the estate’s last high-rise residential plot, with the remaining plots expected to be set aside for low-rise housing to match the surrounding landed estate.

The site can accommodate three 27-storey towers with 562 units. Named Lentor Signature, the project is likely to launch in 2027. Once completed, GuocoLand will have had a hand in five of the eight sites launched at Lentor Hills, shaping much of the new precinct.

When no one else bids

GuocoLand has also been the sole bidder for several Government Land Sale (GLS) sites in recent years. In 2023, GuocoLand and Hong Leong Holdings were the only bidders for the Lentor Gardens site. That site was launched in March 2024 as the 533-unit Lentor Mansion, which was 75% sold over its launch weekend. It was fully sold in November 2025 at an average of $2,255 psf.

GuocoLand was also the sole bidder for the Springleaf site. The 941-unit Springleaf Residence sold 92% of its units over its launch weekend in August 2025, and is now 98.7% sold at an average of $2,179 psf.

A lack of rival bids does not change the developer’s assessment of a project. “As long as we’re satisfied that the site meets all our criteria, we will do it,” says Cheng.

Nor does competition put it off: the River Modern site drew five bids when its tender closed in February 2025.

Its latest sole bid was for a waterfront site at Berlayar Drive. A joint venture between GuocoLand and Hong Leong Holdings was the only bidder when the tender closed in August, winning the site for $576.78 million (1,515 psf ppr). The development is expected to yield about 415 homes.

The site near Keppel Bay is within walking distance of Telok Blangah MRT Station. It is also adjacent to Bukit Chermin, a forested area with heritage bungalows. Cheng says it offers the chance to create “a very unique waterfront product, which is low-rise and surrounded by nature”.

From buildings to neighbourhoods

Guoco Tower , a mixed-use development at Tanjong Pagar completed in 2016, marked a major step in the group’s transformation. It was the seed of an investment portfolio that stood at $6.86 billion as at June 30, 2026. Together with its development business, the portfolio forms GuocoLand’s “twin engine” model, balancing recurring rental income with development earnings.

GuocoLand followed up Guoco Tower with Guoco Midtown, built on a white site which it won in a GLS tender in 2017. Guoco Midtown is connected to the 558-unit Midtown Modern residences on Tan Quee Lan Street. When the group first evaluated the site, Cheng recalls, the area already had a mix of offices, hotels and entertainment venues. It is also near educational institutions such as Nanyang Academy of Fine Arts, LaSalle College of the Arts, School of the Arts and Singapore Management University.

The location’s youthful, vibrant population convinced Cheng that it could support a premium Grade A office development, even though it was not an established office precinct.

The name “Midtown” was inspired by global cities such as New York, which has a downtown, midtown and uptown. Cheng hopes the name will eventually belong to the wider Bugis-Beach Road area, not just GuocoLand’s development, so that the precinct becomes known as Singapore’s Midtown.

Recently completed pedestrian bridges now connect Guoco Midtown with the redeveloped Shaw Tower next door and Suntec City across Nicoll Highway, knitting the precinct together.

Making places come alive

A successful urban destination takes more than attractive buildings. A less visible but important part of GuocoLand’s work is what Cheng calls place management.

It begins at the design stage, with careful thought given to public spaces, pedestrian flow, retail and comfort. The aim is a “baseline of vibrancy”: a steady stream of people using the spaces even when no programmes or events are running, says Cheng.

At Guoco Midtown, for example, computational fluid dynamics studies guided the design of shelters and the placement of fans to improve airflow and keep the outdoor areas comfortable.

Design is only the start. Once a development is completed, the management team watches how people use the spaces, introduces activities and adjusts accordingly. Sometimes users decide how a place evolves, says Cheng.

At Guoco Tower’s urban park, for instance, the team noticed people gathering to eat, work and catch up with friends, so it added more tables and chairs.

At the newly completed Lentor Modern mall, place management is still in its early stages. Cheng expects the retail mix and activities to evolve as the neighbourhood matures and the team learns more about local preferences. “It is not an overnight thing,” he says.

Taking a long-term view means choosing timeless architecture, along with materials and fixtures that are easy to maintain, Cheng says. It also means thinking about the communities that will eventually live and work in each development.

What sets a successful developer apart, he believes, is the discipline to approach every project with fresh eyes. “Every project that we do, we start from first principles,” he says.

title: City Developments Ltd's pioneering spirit drives decade-long reign as Top Developer
article:
When property giant City Developments Ltd (CDL) launched the 1,111-unit The Sail @ Marina Bay in 2004, it was the first major residential project in Singapore’s new downtown.

The Marina Bay Sands integrated resort had not yet been announced, and living in the heart of the financial district was largely untested. Yet CDL saw an opportunity to pioneer a new concept of inner-city living.

Designed by the late Peter Pran of US architectural firm NBBJ, The Sail would become a defining landmark on the Marina Bay skyline.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

More than two decades later, CDL continues to be a trailblazer, from embarking on large-scale mixed-use developments to transforming ageing commercial districts to exploring emerging residential segments.

That pioneering spirit has been a recurring theme in CDL’s history, and it is reflected in its awards record. At the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026, CDL won the Top Developer award for the 10th consecutive year, making it the only developer to have taken the title every year since the awards began in 2017. To mark the milestone, it received the inaugural Decade of Excellence Award.

CDL was also named Top Sustainable Developer and won 13 more awards for its residential developments, including Zyon Grand and Newport Residences .

“We will continue to transform our city and shape our skyline with bold architectural design and innovative lifestyle concepts,” says Chia Ngiang Hong, group general manager of CDL.

Reimagining the city centre

As it did with The Sail, CDL is again betting on city living. This time, it is doing so by transforming older commercial buildings.

With Singapore seeking to rejuvenate its ageing commercial districts and bring more homes into the CBD, CDL has been among the developers to take up the government’s CBD Incentive and Strategic Development Incentive schemes, which grant additional gross floor area (GFA) for redeveloping older buildings.

“Strategic government initiatives present prime opportunities to unlock hidden value in underutilised or ageing assets while rejuvenating central districts,” says Chia.

Newport Plaza and Union Square show how. Redeveloped under the CBD Incentive Scheme, Newport Plaza replaces Fuji Xerox Towers . The former office building on Anson Road was developed by CDL and completed in 1987.

For Union Square, CDL combined its Central Mall with the neighbouring Central Square , which it bought from Far East Organization for $315 million in 2021, and redeveloped both. Union Square is the first redevelopment in the Singapore River planning area under the Strategic Development Incentive Scheme.

At both sites, the incentive schemes allowed CDL to achieve substantial GFA uplifts and create mixed-use developments combining offices, retail and homes.

The bet is paying off. The freehold, 124-unit Newport Residences sold 57% of its units at its launch in January, and was 83.3% sold by Nov 1, at an average of $3,166 psf, based on caveats lodged.

The 366-unit, 99-year leasehold Union Square Residences was launched in November 2024. It is 73% sold at an average of $3,044 psf as at Nov 1.

Venturing into new residential segments

CDL has also moved quickly into new segments of the housing market. Zyon Grand, a joint venture with Mitsui Fudosan (Asia), sits on the Zion Road (Parcel A) Government Land Sale (GLS) site, which was earmarked for Singapore’s first long-stay serviced apartments under the new SA2 category. The two partners were the only bidders.

The mixed-use development comprises the Zyon Galleria retail podium, directly linked to Havelock MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, twin residential towers with 706 units, and a 36-storey block with 373 serviced apartments.

At its October 2025 launch, Zyon Grand sold 84% of its residential units at an average of $3,050 psf. By Nov 1, it was more than 90% sold at an average of $3,067 psf, based on caveats lodged.

Although SA2 is new to Singapore, CDL is no stranger to the wider living sector. Since entering it in 2018, the group has built a global portfolio of private rented sector (PRS) co-living, multi-family housing and purpose-built student accommodation totalling 7,608 units and beds, with a gross development value of $3.7 billion.

“Our move into the SA2 serviced apartment category at Zyon Grand reflects our strategic vision to expand our living sector portfolio and build a strong recurring income platform,” says Chia.

Being the sole bidder for an untested concept carries risk. “We de-risk new concepts through exhaustive evaluation of urban planning, infrastructure and demographic trends,” he says.

History of breaking new ground

Founded in 1963, CDL has grown into one of Singapore’s largest listed property groups, with residential, commercial and hospitality interests in 167 locations across 28 countries. Its evolution has spanned three generations of the Kwek family, from the late Kwek Hong Png, founder of Hong Leong Group, to  executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng and his son, group CEO Sherman Kwek.

The group’s appetite for new residential concepts predates its recent ventures into urban renewal and long-stay serviced apartments. In July 2006, it launched St Regis Residences, Singapore’s first hotel-branded residential development. The 999-year leasehold, 173-unit project brought the hospitality services of the luxury hotel brand to private homes.

That same month, CDL won The Quayside Collection site at Sentosa Cove under the government’s two-envelope tender system, in which bids are judged on design and concept before price.

The site has since become an integrated waterfront destination comprising the 228-unit The Residences at W Singapore Sentosa Cove, the adjacent 240-room W Singapore – Sentosa Cove hotel, and Quayside Isle, an upscale dining and lifestyle hub fronting the marina.

Another landmark is South Beach , which CDL also won under the two-envelope tender system.

Developed with Malaysia’s IOI Properties Group and completed in 2016, the large-scale mixed-use project comprises a Grade A office tower, the 634-room JW Marriott Hotel Singapore South Beach, the 190-unit South Beach Residences and a retail podium directly linked to Esplanade MRT Station on the Circle Line. IOI bought out CDL’s stake in 2025.

“At CDL, we view large-scale and mixed-use projects not simply as real estate developments, but as catalysts for living ecosystems and placemaking,” says Chia.

More recently, CDL partnered with CapitaLand to redevelop the former Liang Court at Clarke Quay into CanningHill Piers and CanningHill Square. Designed by Danish architecture firm Bjarke Ingels Group, the development comprises the 696-unit CanningHill Piers condo, Somerset Singapore Serviced Residence, Moxy Singapore Clarke Quay hotel and a two-storey retail and F&B podium.

The retail and hospitality components have opened in phases since mid-2024, and CanningHill Piers is expected to obtain its temporary occupation permit by end-2026.

Innovation as a constant

CDL’s pioneering approach extends beyond new development concepts to construction methods, sustainability and building design.

The group adopted its environmental ethos of “Conserving as we construct” in 1995, long before sustainability became a mainstream consideration in property development.

The Brownstone, an executive condo (EC) launched in 2015, was Singapore’s first private development to adopt prefabricated prefinished volumetric construction, in which building modules are manufactured off-site and assembled on-site.

The developer subsequently raised the bar for sustainable design with Copen Grand, the first EC to achieve the Building and Construction Authority’s Green Mark Platinum Super Low Energy rating and Maintainability Badge. At Norwood Grand in Woodlands, CDL also introduced on-site 3D concrete printing for the development’s childcare centre.

CDL has also adapted its residential designs to changing homebuyer preferences. Newer developments such as Tembusu Grand, CanningHill Piers and Newport Residences feature biophilic landscaping and co-working spaces. As apartments become more compact, CDL has focused on flexible layouts and generous communal amenities.

Staying the course in the EC market

While few major listed developers still build ECs, CDL remains active in the segment, catering to HDB upgraders and young families seeking private condo living at more accessible prices.

“ECs serve an essential role in Singapore’s housing landscape, bridging public housing and private condos,” says Chia.

The EC segment also gives the group stability, he adds, with steady sales across property cycles from a large pool of eligible owner-occupiers.

CDL’s recent ECs have been well received. The 639-unit Copen Grand was sold out within a month of its launch in October 2022. Meanwhile, the 512-unit  Lumina Grand was fully sold within 18 months of its January 2024 launch.

Building on that momentum, CDL secured two more EC sites at Woodlands Drive 17 and Senja Close in August 2025, ahead of the EC measures announced in May this year. The new rules, which include doubling the minimum occupation period from five to 10 years, apply to projects on sites whose land tenders closed on or after May 8, 2026.

CDL’s two upcoming ECs, Wynwood Grand and Solano Grand, which were acquired before that date, will therefore remain under the previous rules. Both are slated for launch in 1Q2027. The two ECs are among four projects CDL plans to launch in 2027, totalling about 1,630 units.

Taking the long view

Partnerships have also been central to how CDL manages development risks and takes on increasingly complex projects. Over the years, it has worked with developers and construction groups including CapitaLand, Frasers Property , Sekisui House, Sunway MCL and, more recently, Woh Hup Holdings.

Its partnership with Mitsui Fudosan (Asia) at Zyon Grand builds on a relationship dating back more than five decades. In 1972, Mitsui Fudosan and Hong Leong Group formed TID as an equal joint venture.

A year later, TID joined CDL and Hong Leong Holdings to form Tripartite Developers, which went on to develop the Flora Drive private residential enclave off Upper Changi Road North.

Looking ahead, Chia expects developers to be judged on more than location and design. “In the coming decade, we believe a successful developer will be distinguished by its ability to anticipate changing needs, lead in decarbonisation, execute complex urban regeneration and build resilient recurring income streams,” he says.

It has been a long way from 2004, when CDL took a chance on downtown living with The Sail. Twenty-two years on, homes have become a familiar part of the city centre, with more sites released in Marina Bay and older CBD office buildings redeveloped into mixed-use developments, including residences.

“By taking a multigenerational view, we align our developments with Singapore’s long-term urban transformation plans,” says Chia. “Ultimately, we hope to create developments that not only meet the needs of today’s buyers, but also remain relevant, resilient and valuable for many generations to come.”

title: Singapore REITs Are Down: Which 3 Could Recover First?
article:
Investors in Singapore real estate investment trusts (REITs) have had a rough year thus far.
As at 5 November 2026, the
CSOP iEdge S-REIT Leaders Index ETF
(SGX: SRT) is down 11% year-to-date (YTD) against a 13.7% gain for the broader
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI)
So, are
REITs
worth a second look?
Maybe, but a rebound won’t lift them all equally.
The ones with solid balance sheets, dependable rent and an upcoming catalyst should move first.
In this article, we spotlight three REITs that fit that description in different ways, which could stand to benefit once sentiment for the industry turns around.

(SGX: CRPU).
Parkway Life REIT, or PLife REIT – As safe as it gets
PLife REIT owns Singapore hospitals, alongside nursing homes in Japan and France.
Its balance sheet is the strongest here; leverage is low at 33.8%.
Meanwhile, interest is covered over 8.2x with an all-in borrowing cost of just 1.67%, and about 96% of its rate exposure is hedged.
Its weighted average debt maturity will extend to 3.6 years once a maturing loan is refinanced.
The recurring rental income it earns is about as locked in as REIT income gets.
Leases average 14.6 years and most come with built-in annual rental escalations.
These features helped lift DPU 14.6% to S$0.0877 in 1H2026 (ended 30 June 2026), adding to steady growth since its 2007 listing.
Occupancy is 100% in both Singapore and France, while Japan trails at 94.3% after a tenant exited five nursing homes, which weighed on revenue.
Looking forward, the main catalysts for PLife REIT come from continued rent increases across its properties and the potential expansion into more European markets or the UK, which management is studying.
The key risk would be
higher interest rates
, which could increase financing costs and put some downward pressure on unit prices.
Regardless, given the strength of its balance sheet, PLife REIT could be the first to benefit when sentiment turns.
Keppel DC REIT, or KDCREIT – Riding the Data Centre Boom
KDCREIT owns
data centres
in Asia Pacific and Europe, where demand is still running hot.
Its rents show it.
Rental renewals in 9M2026 (ended 30 September 2026) were signed at about 14% higher rates, pushing DPU up 11.7% to S$0.08571.
Occupancy improved slightly to 93.0%.
Cardiff continues to be unoccupied, so a new tenant there would lift income.
Leases average 6.5 years by space, and gearing of 36.2% (38.8% after its latest Tokyo purchase) leaves room for more acquisitions.
The catch is concentration.
Internet companies account for 70.2% of rental income, and the REIT’s single largest tenant alone accounts for more than 40%.
A slowdown in rental growth could also pressure DPU growth moving forward.
Management is also studying power upgrades and redevelopment at older sites, which could add income but would mean more capital spending.
The upside? Continued momentum in rental growth, higher occupancy rates and more accretive acquisitions.
KDCREIT doesn’t really need a sector rally to grow, because rising rents can lift its earnings largely on their own; nevertheless, a sector rally could see KDCREIT be among the first beneficiaries.
Sasseur REIT – Cheap, but There’s a Reason
Sasseur REIT owns four outlet malls in China.
At about S$0.61 as of 4 November 2026, it offers a yield of about 10.7% and trades below its NAV of S$0.82 per unit.
Debt isn’t why it’s cheap.
Gearing sits at just 25.6%, borrowing costs have fallen to a low of 3.7%, and its average debt maturity is decent at 4.8 years, with no refinancing requirement until 2030.
The discount is about China.
Sasseur’s rent comes from an agreement with its outlet operator that combines a fixed amount, rising 3% a year, with a share of sales.
Tenant sales have held up, reaching a record RMB 2.3 billion in 1H2026 (ended 30 June 2026), up 7.4%, and DPU rose 10.2% to S$0.03366.
Leases with the brands inside its malls are short, though, averaging 1.5 years by space.
Its income is also in RMB, so a weaker RMB reduces both its distributions and NAV in Singapore-dollar terms.
A slowdown in Chinese spending would hit both rent and property values, which could mean lower payouts.
A consumer-targeted stimulus by the government and lower rates, on the other hand, could narrow the gap to NAV.
The cheapest of the three, Sasseur has the most potential upside if you’re willing to underwrite the China risk; its 10.7% yield is the incentive for investors.
What Could Delay a REIT Recovery?
A rebound isn’t guaranteed.
If interest rates stay high, refinancing will keep eating into distributions.
Weaker tenant demand or negative rental reversions would hurt income, and more DPU cuts across the sector would keep investors wary.
Lower property values would also push gearing up.
Investors may also keep favouring banks and growth stocks, which have done much better this year.
A steep fall in a REIT’s unit price doesn’t automatically mean a recovery will follow.
Get Smart: Look for the REITs With a Catalyst
A REIT recovery, when it comes, probably won’t be even.
Parkway Life looks the steadiest candidate, while KDCREIT has rental growth on its side, and Sasseur REIT has the most room to rise if its discount narrows.
Rather than buying whatever has fallen furthest, ask what could actually push a REIT’s income and valuation higher.
The ones with a clear answer deserve a closer look.
